outcome: ability to distinguish RhIG from true anti-D antibodies
diagnosis of clinically significant anti-D antibody
Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)
cohort: The retrospective review included 348 samples identified as RhIG and 52 true anti-D samples from medical records, preceded by a case report of a pregnant patient with a missed anti-D antibody and her anemic infant.
finding: Agglutination strength alone does not provide reliable evidence to distinguish RhIG from high titer anti-D antibodies, as 6% of RhIG samples showed 3+ strength and 44.4% of high titer anti-D samples showed 1+ or 2+ reactivity.
